outcome: No proof, disproof, or rigorous partial resolution of the base-10 Lychrel number existence question has appeared since 26 January 2024. The only in-window publication found (Kuitché, Advances in Pure Mathematics, August 2024) offers a probabilistic/heuristic argument, not a rigorous proof, and its own author explicitly states the characterization 'remains probabilistic' and that no particular natural number has been proven Lychrel.
summary: The question 'do any base-10 Lychrel numbers exist?' remains open. I checked the English Wikipedia article on Lychrel numbers (current version), which still states no base-10 Lychrel number has been proven to exist. I examined the one paper the triage flagged — Rostand S. Kuitché, 'Lychrel Numbers in Base 10: A Probabilistic Approach' (Advances in Pure Mathematics, Vol. 14 No. 8, August 2024) — by fetching the paper page directly rather than trusting the triage's title-only note. It proposes a probabilistic definition of 'Lychrel' (probability of ever reaching a palindrome falling below (1/10)^330) and a theorem relating this to a limiting growth ratio, and tests specific numbers (196, 879, 1997, 7059) computationally using ordinary iterative code ('Anaconda Navigator', no AI/ML). The author explicitly acknowledges the result is not a rigorous existence proof for any particular number and calls the probabilistic characterization a limitation to be addressed in future work. Under §3.1, a probabilistic/heuristic argument that does not settle any case or the general question is not a result that changes what a careful person would write in this bullet — it is at most an unproven conjecture-supporting heuristic, so it does not even rise to 'progress' on a bound (there is no bound here — this is a yes/no existence question, and per §3.1 an existence question only moves when actually answered). I also checked for any updates to the long-running '196 Palindrome Quest' record computations (Jason Doucette's world-records page, p196.org's news page): the most recent record and news entries found date to 2011–2016 (Romain Dolbeau's billion-iteration, ~414-million-digit computation; a 2016 note about a German student group), with nothing newer located, and in any case a longer non-palindromic run is a search-limit extension, not an answer to the existence question, so it would not count as an event even if a 2024–2026 update existed. I searched broadly for any AI/LLM/ML connection (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, GPT, general 'machine learning' searches) and found none tying any AI system to Lychrel numbers; all computational work found (the 2024 paper's code, the historical palindrome-quest programs) is ordinary iterative/brute-force computation, not an AI system under §6.2. I did encounter one WebSearch AI-generated summary that conflated an unrelated arXiv paper (on the Tribonacci sequence) with the Lychrel paper, and another that vaguely asserted existence had been 'proven in base 2, 11, or 17' — the latter refers to other numeral bases, not base 10, and predates the window in any case, so it is irrelevant to this bullet's base-10 statement. Overall: no change found, no AI involvement found.
competing_reading: One could argue the August 2024 paper constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense (a novel probabilistic framework and equivalence theorem), which might warrant status 'progress' rather than 'open'. I read it as not qualifying because 'progress' under this schema is reserved for a bound moving or an instructive incident on a question with a bound to move, whereas this is a binary existence question that only moves when answered (§3.1's existence-question rule), and the paper itself disclaims proving existence for any concrete number or in general. If a future reviewer judges the probabilistic theorem itself to be a form of admissible progress on the framework (even without an existence proof), 'progress' with ai_role 'none' would be the alternate classification.
what_would_settle_it: A rigorous (deterministic) proof that some specific base-10 number is Lychrel (or a proof that no base-10 Lychrel numbers exist), published or preprinted after 26 January 2024 and ideally digested by an expert or verified computationally/formally; absent that, any credible claim — even an unresolved or later-withdrawn one — naming a specific number and a non-probabilistic argument would at minimum warrant a 'claimed' or 'progress'/'incident' status.
